prompt: The Grand Canyon stretches in layered bands of red, orange, and cream sandstone from the South Rim to the North Rim under a midday sky of deep blue and scattered white cloud. Every stratum is sharp and legible—the Kaibab limestone at the rim, the Coconino sandstone below, the Redwall limestone cliffs, and the dark Vishnu schist at the river's gorge. The Colorado River is a thin green thread at the canyon floor, and the flat-topped mesas and erosion-carved temples fill the middle distance. The light is even and high, casting short shadows that define each ledge and talus slope with equal clarity.

Victoria Falls plunges into the Batoka Gorge along a mile-wide basalt lip, the curtain of white water dropping three hundred feet into a chasm so deep the spray rises back above the rim in a permanent column of mist. The falls' individual cataracts, the black basalt edge, the rainforest clinging to the gorge walls, and the rainbow arcing through the spray are all uniformly sharp. The Zambezi above the falls is a wide, flat expanse of dark water broken by rocky islands, and the sky above is clear and blue, the mist column catching the sunlight in a pillar of white and prismatic colour.

The Salar de Uyuni stretches to every horizon as a perfectly flat expanse of white hexagonal salt tiles under a sky of intense blue. The salt crust's geometric cracking pattern is sharp and detailed from the immediate foreground to the vanishing distance, and the Tunupa volcano rises from the salt flat's northern edge in a cone of brown and white. Only the infinite white plain meeting the blue sky in a razor-sharp line, and the midday sun creating short, hard shadows in the cracks between the salt polygons.

Zhangjiajie's sandstone pillar forest rises from a sea of green canopy in Hunan province, hundreds of narrow quartzite columns standing hundreds of metres tall, their flat tops crowned with twisted pines and trailing vines. Every pillar from the nearest to the most distant is sharp and distinct, the gaps between them revealing layer after layer of receding columns fading only in atmospheric haze, not in focus. Wisps of cloud thread between the pillars at mid-height, and the canopy below is a dense, unbroken green. The light is soft and overcast, eliminating harsh shadows and rendering the stone in uniform tones of grey, ochre, and rust.

The Northern Lights fill the sky above a black volcanic beach in Iceland in sweeping curtains of green, violet, and white. The aurora's bands are sharp-edged and vivid, and the basalt sea stacks of Reynisdrangar stand as dark silhouettes against the glowing sky. The wet black sand reflects the green light in a broad mirror, and the surf line is a faint white fringe at the water's edge. Every element from the foreground pebbles to the distant headland and the stars visible between the aurora bands is in equal focus, the scene lit entirely by the aurora and a thin crescent moon.

The Twelve Apostles limestone stacks stand in the Southern Ocean surf along Victoria's coastline under a dramatic sky of charcoal cloud broken by shafts of golden light. The stacks' sheer cliff faces, the layered sandstone striations, and the wave-carved arches at their bases are uniformly sharp, and the turquoise-and-white surf wraps around each pillar in detailed foam patterns. The ochre cliffs of the coastline stretch in both directions, and the light isolates two of the stacks in golden sun while the others remain in cool blue shadow.

Plitvice Lakes cascade through a series of sixteen terraced turquoise pools connected by hundreds of waterfalls in a forested Croatian valley. The travertine barriers between each pool, the moss and the mineral deposits, and the submerged fallen logs in the crystal-clear water are all equally sharp. The surrounding beech and fir forest is in full autumn colour—gold, russet, and dark green—and the waterfalls range from wide curtains to thin threads, all frozen sharp in the even overcast light. The water's colour shifts from pale aquamarine in the shallows to deep teal in the pools.

The Giant's Causeway extends into the grey North Atlantic as a pavement of forty thousand interlocking hexagonal basalt columns, their flat tops forming a stepping-stone surface from the cliff base to the waterline. Each column's geometric facets, the rusty iron staining in the joints, and the sea spray pooling in the tops are uniformly in focus. The basalt cliff behind rises in columnar tiers like an organ pipe facade, and the surf wraps around the causeway's outermost columns in white foam. The sky is heavy and overcast, the light flat and cool, rendering the basalt in tones of charcoal, steel, and dull amber.

The Painted Desert of Arizona stretches in horizontal bands of red, lavender, grey, and white bentonite clay under a vast sky of pale blue and high cirrus. The badlands' eroded ridges, the flat-topped mesas, and the dry wash channels are uniformly in focus from the nearest cracked mudflat to the distant Chinle formation cliffs. No vegetation interrupts the mineral palette, and the midday sun lights the clay from directly above, letting the colours read as pure pigment—brick red beside cool lavender beside chalky white in repeating sedimentary layers.

Ha Long Bay's limestone karsts rise from emerald water in their hundreds, each island a vertical tower of grey rock topped with dense jungle green. Every karst from the nearest—close enough to see the barnacle line and the cave mouths at waterline—to the most distant is sharp and detailed, the formations receding into a soft atmospheric haze that is tonal, not optical. The water between the islands is flat and glassy, reflecting each karst as a dark inverted twin, and a pale morning sky holds the faintest blush of pink at the eastern horizon.

A braided glacial river spreads across a black volcanic outwash plain in Iceland, dozens of intertwining channels of milky grey-blue meltwater cutting through the dark basalt sand. Every channel, gravel bar, and silt deposit is uniformly sharp from the nearest rivulet to the distant glacier tongue and the surrounding mountains. The river plain stretches miles wide, the only colour the faint blue of the glacial water against the charcoal earth and the white of the glacier above. The sky is low and overcast, the light even and cool, rendering the landscape in a stark palette of black, grey, white, and glacial blue.

The Matterhorn rises as a near-perfect pyramid of dark rock and snow above an alpine meadow, the east face in full morning sun, the north face in blue shadow. The ridgelines—the Hörnli, the Zmuttgrat, the Furgggrat, and the Italian ridge—are all sharp and defined, and the glacier at the base is a cracked field of blue-white ice. The alpine meadow in the foreground holds the last wildflowers of summer, and every element from the nearest gentian to the summit rocks is in equal, unforgiving focus against a sky of deep cobalt.

A turquoise hot spring steams in a Yellowstone geyser basin, the mineral-stained rings of orange, white, and emerald terracing outward from the boiling centre to the cooler edges. The surrounding basin is a vast plain of white silica flats stretching to distant lodgepole pine forest under a cold blue sky, and the steam column rises straight and thick from the spring's eye. Every mineral deposit, every thermophile colour band, and every crack in the sinter crust is uniformly sharp, and the low winter sun paints the steam in gold against the dark treeline.

The Banaue rice terraces descend in two-thousand-year-old steps from a cloud-forest ridge to the river valley below in the Philippine Cordillera, each terrace wall a precise curve of hand-stacked stone holding a shallow pool of water that mirrors the sky. The green rice shoots, the stone retaining walls, and the moss-covered irrigation channels are all uniformly sharp from the nearest paddy to the distant ridge. The valley holds a thin layer of morning mist, the surrounding peaks are dark with forest, and the overcast light renders every terrace step with equal clarity.

An immense tabletop iceberg floats in the Antarctic Sound, its sheer blue-white cliff face rising forty metres from the steel-grey water, the waterline undercut carved by the tide, and the turquoise glow of compressed ancient ice visible where a section has recently calved. The Southern Ocean stretches flat behind it to a distant ice shelf on the horizon, and every crystal in the ice face, every wave lapping the berg's base, and every distant crevasse in the shelf is uniformly in focus. The sky is a pale overcast, and the iceberg's shadow on the water is a deep blue-green rectangle.

Wadi Rum's sandstone desert stretches in a vast plain of red-orange sand punctuated by monolithic jebels—sheer-sided rock formations rising hundreds of metres from the flat valley floor. The nearest jebel's wind-eroded mushroom base, the Nabataean rock-cut channels on its face, and the distant formations lined along the horizon are all equally sharp. The sand is rippled by wind into parallel ridges, and the sky is enormous—deep blue overhead fading to a hot white at the horizon where the sand and sky merge. The late afternoon sun rakes across the formations, painting one side amber and leaving the other in cool purple shadow.

Lake Baikal in winter is a vast frozen plain of clear black ice, the surface cracked into geometric pressure ridges and turquoise fissures that reveal the extreme depth below. The ice's surface texture, the trapped methane bubbles frozen in vertical columns, and the snow-dusted pressure ridges are uniformly in focus from the immediate foreground to the distant Siberian mountains ringing the shore. The sky is pale and cold, and the low sun catches the ice cracks in veins of electric blue against the otherwise transparent black surface. The scale is oceanic—the far shore is barely visible as a white line of snow.

The Danakil Depression in Ethiopia spreads as a surreal landscape of acid-green sulphur pools, white salt flats, and rust-orange iron deposits under a sky bleached white by heat. The hydrothermal vents bubble in emerald-green pools rimmed with bright yellow sulphur crystals, and the surrounding salt crust is cracked into polygonal tiles of pure white. Every crystal formation, every bubbling vent, and every colour transition from green to yellow to orange is uniformly sharp, and the horizon shimmers with heat distortion but the foreground mineral formations are rendered in clinical, unforgiving detail.

Antelope Canyon's slot walls rise forty feet on both sides, the Navajo sandstone carved into smooth flowing curves by millennia of flash floods. A beam of midday light penetrates the narrow opening above and strikes the canyon floor, illuminating the sand in a blinding white spot while the surrounding walls glow in reflected amber, coral, and deep violet. The rock's layered striations swirl like frozen liquid, and every grain of the sandstone texture, every ripple in the sculpted wall, and every fine sand particle suspended in the light beam is uniformly sharp from the nearest curve to the farthest visible bend.

The Dolomites' Tre Cime di Lavaredo stand as three sheer limestone towers against a twilight sky, the vertical north faces in deep blue shadow, the upper rims catching the last horizontal light in a thin line of warm gold. The alpine scree field in the foreground is a uniform grey slope of broken rock, and a small glacial tarn at the towers' base reflects the sky in a dark oval mirror. Every crack in the limestone face, every boulder on the scree, and every ripple on the tarn's surface is in equal focus, and the sky above holds the first visible stars and a gradient from warm amber at the western horizon to deep indigo overhead.
